\chapter{One, Two, Three}
\label{ch:ge-zahlen-1-3}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count one, two, three in German and say why each is the English number's twin rather than a Latin borrowing.}

The first three numbers, one per lesson, and then the sound law that explains every difference between them and their English twins. German's numbers were never borrowed from Latin; this chapter is where that stops being a claim and becomes something the reader can hear.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[eins]{eins — \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} and the German \emph{ei}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-eins}



\begin{quote}
Here is where German is closer to English than any Romance language gets. Its numbers are not borrowed from Latin — they are German's own, and they are the near-twins of the English ones. Start with the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: eins}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{eins} — \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} the number you say when you are counting.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — German \textbf{ei} is the English word \textbf{eye}. Always, in every word, with no exceptions to remember.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{eins} is \emph{eyns}. You already own this one: \emph{heißen} is \emph{HY-ssen}, and \emph{Wiedersehen} has an \emph{ie}, which is the other way round and says \emph{ee}. \textbf{ei} says \emph{eye}; \textbf{ie} says \emph{ee}. The second letter tells you which.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{eins} is English \textbf{one}. Not borrowed from it, not similar to it — the same inherited word, which is why it needs no story to make it stick.

English hides the relationship in its spelling. \emph{One} is written as though it rhymed with \emph{bone}, and it did once; the \emph{w}-sound at the front (\emph{wun}) crept in later. Strip that off and \emph{one} and \emph{ein} are the same shape.

The same word is also sitting inside English \textbf{a} and \textbf{an} — \emph{an apple} is \emph{one apple}, worn down. German does exactly the same thing with \emph{eins}, and once the first five are learned there is a lesson on it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} — \emph{eyns}, with the English word \emph{eye} inside it
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} — the same old word
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ei\textquotedblright{} as \emph{eye}, \textquotedblleft{}ie\textquotedblright{} as \emph{ee} — the second letter decides
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} in German? (\emph{Eins}.) How is \textbf{ei} said? (Like the English word \emph{eye}.) And \textbf{ie}? (\emph{Ee}.) Which English word is \emph{eins}? (\emph{One} — and \emph{a}/\emph{an} underneath it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zwei]{zwei — \textquotedblleft{}two,\textquotedblright{} and the \emph{z} that is a \emph{ts}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-zwei}



\begin{quote}
One down. The second number has the same \emph{ei} you just learned, and one letter that does not say what an English reader expects.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: zwei}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{zwei} — \textquotedblleft{}two.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{tsvy}. The \textbf{z} is the \emph{ts} of English \emph{cats} — never the buzz of English \emph{zoo}. That is the whole of the German \textbf{z}: it has one job and it never does anything else.

The other two letters you already own. The \textbf{w} is a \emph{v}, as in \emph{wohnen}, and the \textbf{ei} is \emph{eye}, as in \emph{eins}. So \emph{zwei} is three rules you have and one that is new.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{zwei} is English \textbf{two}, with the \emph{tw-} opening turned into \emph{zw-}.

English still says the \emph{tw-} out loud in the words \emph{two} grew from — \textbf{twin} (two born together), \textbf{between} (in the space of two), \textbf{twice}, \textbf{twenty}. It only lost the \emph{w} in the number itself, which is why \emph{two} is spelt with a letter nobody pronounces. German kept the pair and shifted the \emph{t} to \emph{ts}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{tw-} $\to$ \emph{zw-}: \textbf{two} / \emph{zwei}, \textbf{twin} / \emph{Zwilling}, \textbf{twelve} / \emph{zwölf}
\end{quote}

So the silent \emph{w} in English \textbf{two} is not a spelling accident. It is the \emph{w} that German still says.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}zwei\textquotedblright{} — \emph{tsvy}, the \emph{z} like the end of \emph{cats}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}twin\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}zwei\textquotedblright{}, and hear the \emph{w} come back
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Zwei}.) How is German \textbf{z} said? (\emph{Ts}, as in \emph{cats}.) Which English words still say the \emph{w} that \emph{two} dropped? (\emph{Twin}, \emph{between}, \emph{twice}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[drei]{drei — \textquotedblleft{}three,\textquotedblright{} and German's missing \emph{th}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-drei}



\begin{quote}
Third number, third \emph{ei}. And it shows you something that will keep paying: German has no \textbf{th} sound at all, and you can predict what it uses instead.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: drei}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{drei} — \textquotedblleft{}three.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Said \emph{dry}: the scraped \emph{r} you met in \emph{lernen}, and the \emph{ei} saying \emph{eye}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{drei} is English \textbf{three}. German simply has no \emph{th}, and where English says one, German says \textbf{d}. That is not a fact about numbers — it is a fact about the whole language, and you have been using it since your first \emph{danke}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{German} \\
\midrule
\textbf{th}ree & \textbf{d}rei \\
\textbf{th}e & \textbf{d}er, \textbf{d}ie, \textbf{d}as \\
\textbf{th}ank & \textbf{d}anke \\
\textbf{th}at & \textbf{d}as \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five words, one swap. Whenever an English word starts with \emph{th}, try a \emph{d} and you will often land on the German.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}drei\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dry}, scrape the \emph{r}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei\textquotedblright{}
  \item the swap — \textquotedblleft{}three/drei\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}the/der\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}thank/danke\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Drei}.) What does German use where English has \textbf{th}? (\textbf{D}.) Give three pairs. (\emph{Three/drei}, \emph{the/der}, \emph{thank/danke}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(siblings, not borrowings)]{Siblings, not borrowings}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-grimm}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Drei}, \emph{three}, and Latin \emph{tres} all mean three and all start with a different sound. Before the next seven numbers, it is worth knowing why — because the answer makes each of them cheaper to learn.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: siblings and cousins}]
German and English are \textbf{siblings}. Latin is a \textbf{cousin}.

That is not a figure of speech. All three grew out of one older language, and Germanic — the parent of English and German — split off from the rest first. So \emph{drei} did not come \textbf{from} \emph{tres}, and English \emph{three} did not either. All three are what one prehistoric word became along three different roads.

Which is why the German numbers are the easy ones and the Romance numbers are the hard ones, for an English speaker: \emph{three} and \emph{drei} are the same word two doors apart, while \emph{tres} is the same word across the street.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The differences are not random. A \textbf{sound law} is a change that happened to \emph{every} word in a language at once, so once you know one you can predict the rest.

You have already met one of these. \emph{Gut} is \emph{good} with the \textbf{d} turned to a \textbf{t}, and \emph{machen} is \emph{make} with the \textbf{k} turned to a \textbf{ch} — one shift, two words, and it caught every word in German that had those sounds.

The shift that separates Germanic from Latin is older and works the same way. The two turns worth carrying into the next lessons are:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Older sound} & \textbf{Germanic sound} & \textbf{Seen in} \\
\midrule
\textbf{t} & \textbf{th}, and German \textbf{d} & Latin \emph{tres}, English \emph{three}, German \emph{drei} \\
\textbf{p} & \textbf{f} & Latin \emph{pes} \textquotedblleft{}foot\textquotedblright{}, English \emph{foot} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So when a Latin word and a German one sound nothing alike, try the first consonant before deciding they are unrelated. Often they are the same word, one law apart.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tres\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}drei\textquotedblright{} — one word, three roads
  \item the two turns — \textquotedblleft{}t becomes th\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}p becomes f\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}good/gut\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}make/machen\textquotedblright{} — the shift you already knew
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{drei} borrowed from Latin \emph{tres}? (No — they are cousins, both from one older word.) What is a sound law? (A change that hit every word in the language at once, so it is predictable.) Which two turns should you carry forward? (Old \textbf{t} to \textbf{th}/\textbf{d}, old \textbf{p} to \textbf{f}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
